Chapter 9: The Role of Intellectuals and Experts in Shaping Opinion
In every society, there are people we naturally turn to for insights and direction—thinkers, experts, and thought leaders. Their words carry real influence, and most of the time, we rarely stop to question their authority. But if you look closer, the part they play in guiding public opinion is a lot more complex than it first appears.
Imagine a well-respected policy analyst, invited to a panel to talk about a current social issue. The room is full of energy, ideas bouncing back and forth. But as the discussion unfolds, the analyst notices something odd—some perspectives just aren’t on the table. The questions seem carefully crafted, always assuming our current institutions are the best starting point. The idea of more radical change? It never even comes up.
What’s really happening here? Too often, the authority of experts is used to reinforce the way things already are. Their knowledge is genuine, and there’s no doubt their intentions are good. But the scope of what they can say—or even consider—gets shaped by the very institutions they work within. So debates end up being about technical tweaks and minor details, while the big, foundational questions are set aside.
Take a scientist, for example, who’s frustrated when their research gets twisted by powerful interests—maybe a corporation, a politician, or a major media outlet. They try to set the record straight, but their voice is drowned out. It becomes clear: having expertise isn’t enough. To really make a difference, you need access to the right platforms, resources, and networks.
Most of us don’t realize how the authority of experts is actually built. We just trust that folks with credentials are looking out for everyone. But in reality, the boundaries of their expertise are shaped by funding, institutional priorities, and the need to stay credible within their own circles.
Now, this doesn’t mean experts can’t be trusted, or that knowledge doesn’t matter. It simply means their role in shaping what we think is always political—whether or not they intend it. The real challenge? Spotting the limits of expertise, questioning the assumptions behind expert opinions, and opening up space for voices that usually go unheard.
If you care about a truly democratic society, here’s what matters: support intellectuals who are willing to push back against the status quo, speak up for justice, and actually connect with the public in a clear and honest way. And just as importantly, let’s value the experience and insight of everyday people—because their voices matter, too, even if they’re not always front and center.
